hook.text: Sugar was rare luxury in 1600. By 1800, British workers ate it daily. Slavery made it cheap.

buildup.text: Caribbean sugar plantations ran on enslaved African labor. Millions died to sweeten European tea.

discovery.text: Historian Sidney Mintz showed sugar transformed from medicine to spice to everyday staple in 200 years.

twist.text: Sugar boycotts became one of the first consumer protest movements. People refused blood-sweetened tea.

climax.text: Every spoonful of sugar carries history. The sweetness was built on the world's bitterest labor.

punchline.text: The sweetest ingredient has the darkest story.

quiz.question: Who wrote about sugar's transformation from luxury to staple?

details.summary: Sugar's history is written in blood. Caribbean sugar plantations were the economic engine of the Atlantic slave trade, with millions of Africans enslaved to satisfy Europe's growing sweet tooth. The profits from sugar funded the Industrial Revolution and shaped the modern world economy.
details.whyItMatters: Sugar connects everyday sweetness to one of history's greatest atrocities. Understanding this link is essential for grasping how racial capitalism shaped the modern world.
takeaways: Sugar plantations drove the majority of the Atlantic slave trade
Caribbean sugar profits funded Britain's Industrial Revolution
Average sugar consumption rose from near-zero to 100+ lbs per person

faq.question: How did sugar drive the slave trade?
faq.answer: Sugar cultivation was brutally labor-intensive — cutting, crushing, and boiling cane in tropical heat. European colonizers established plantations in the Caribbean and Brazil, importing millions of enslaved Africans to work them.

faq.question: How did sugar change European society?
faq.answer: Sugar went from a rare luxury spice to a working-class staple in two centuries. Cheap sugar calories fueled factory workers during industrialization. Tea with sugar became Britain's national drink.
